title: Technical notes on engine shop visits
intro: Short, sourced notes on the decisions that set an engine's cost: removal timing, visit type, workscope, material and lease compliance. Every figure carries its source.

articles.title: Planning shop visits around the 2026 capacity crunch
articles.excerpt: Turnaround times are up 35 per cent for legacy engines and 150 per cent for new-generation types. Planning rules that hold in a constrained market.

sections.heading: Where the numbers stand
paragraphs: Bain's 2024 brief on engine maintenance put the peak of engine MRO demand in 2026 and expects capacity to stay constrained to the end of the decade. Over that period cumulative demand exceeds supply by nearly 17 per cent.

Against pre-pandemic norms, turnaround times are up 35 per cent or more for legacy engines and 150 per cent or more for new-generation engines. Slot waits have lengthened by two to three months, and by up to six in some cases.

Engine-stand data for the first half of 2026 points the same way, unevenly. CFM56-5A/B stand utilisation reached 92 per cent, against 77 per cent in 2025. V2500 project durations rose 9 per cent. CFM56-7B durations fell 17 per cent and LEAP-1A durations fell 8 per cent, so the picture differs by family.

sections.heading: Why the crunch will not clear quickly
paragraphs: Oliver Wyman describes a bow wave of maintenance deferred during the pandemic, which now arrives as bottlenecks, longer turnaround times and fluctuating prices. Delivery delays add to it: 17,000 aircraft orders were unfilled at the start of 2026 and production ended 2025 at 24 per cent below 2019, so older engines fly longer and visit shops more often.

Labour is the slow variable. Bain expects US mechanic demand to grow 4 per cent by 2030 against a 1 per cent rise in the working-age population. Oliver Wyman counts 41 per cent of certified US mechanics over 60, with 45,000 retiring within a decade, and ARSA notes that new technicians need two to five years to reach full productivity.

sections.heading: Five planning rules that hold
paragraphs: Rule one: plan removals from the engine, not the calendar. An engine typically needs three to five shop visits over its life, so each removal date should come from the EGT margin trend, the LLP limits and the slot lead time together, not from a fleet-wide assumption.

Rule two: secure the slot before the workscope is final. With waits of two to six months, the slot request goes out on a provisional workscope and a removal window, and is refined when the engine comes off. Waiting for a perfect workscope costs more than adjusting one.

Rule three: benchmark the quoted turnaround against independent data, not the shop's own history. Acumen's 2026 benchmarks put a CFM56 full overhaul at 90 to 120 days and a light visit near 45; a V2500 at 60 to 70 days; a PW4000 at 120 days or more. A quote far outside these ranges needs an explanation.

Rule four: treat material as part of the schedule. OEM parts demand outpaces supply by 10 to 20 per cent, and used serviceable material covers up to 30 per cent of part demand at some shops. Long-lead parts and repair routes should be identified at table inspection, not discovered at kitting.

Rule five: keep spare-engine cover and lease terms in the same model. A turnaround that slips from 60 to 90 days changes the spare-engine plan and, on a leased aircraft, can move a shop visit across a redelivery date. The model should show both effects before the workscope is approved.

sections.heading: What this means for a managed visit
paragraphs: In a constrained market the value of shop visit management moves earlier: into removal planning, slot negotiation and workscope discipline. On-site presence at induction and table inspection then keeps findings, material decisions and the turnaround plan aligned while the engine is open.

Flight Hour Solution plans removals, negotiates slots and represents clients on site for CFM56, LEAP, V2500 and PW4000 visits. Send us your next workscope and removal window and we will tell you where the turnaround risk sits.

articles.title: Quick-turn, hospital visit or performance restoration?
articles.excerpt: Three visit types, three cost bands and three sets of lease consequences. How the choice is made, and who should be in the room.

sections.heading: Three visits, one engine life
paragraphs: An engine typically needs three to five shop visits over its life. Not all of them are the same event. The industry sorts visits into three types by depth of disassembly: the quick-turn, the hospital visit and the performance restoration. The type decides the workscope, the turnaround, the invoice and, on a leased engine, who pays.

A quick-turn addresses one finding with minimal disassembly: a fan blade set, a gearbox or accessory change, or a borescope finding that can be reached without splitting the core. The engine keeps its remaining life; nothing is restored.

A hospital visit goes deeper to fix a specific problem, often a module removal or a single-module repair, without a full restoration of the engine's performance margins. It buys time on wing but leaves the other modules in their existing condition.

A performance restoration is the full event: the core is disassembled, hot-section parts are inspected and repaired or replaced, life-limited parts at or near their limits are changed, and the engine leaves the test cell with restored EGT margin. It is the multi-million-dollar purchase, typically several million US dollars per visit, and the one that resets the engine's economic clock.

sections.heading: What the choice depends on
paragraphs: The first input is the removal cause. A foreign-object strike on an engine with healthy margins points to a quick-turn. A hot-section distress finding on an engine whose EGT margin has been falling points to restoration, because a repair alone would send it back to the shop within a year or two.

The second input is remaining life. If several life-limited parts have limited cycles left, a hospital visit that ignores them delays a second, unavoidable disassembly. The LLP stub position, cycle by cycle, belongs on the same page as the borescope report.

The third input is cost per cycle rather than cost per visit. Repair costs on the CFM56 have risen 50 to 75 per cent since 2019, hot-section blade prices are up about 30 per cent and fan blade prices have doubled since 2020. In that environment the cheapest visit is rarely the cheapest year.

The fourth input is the shop's turnaround. Independent 2026 benchmarks put a CFM56 full overhaul at 90 to 120 days and a light visit near 45 days; a V2500 at 60 to 70 days. Where slot waits already run two to six months, a restoration must be planned around spare-engine cover, not squeezed into it.

sections.heading: Why the lease cares
paragraphs: Lease documents draw the same line in their own language. Many define an Engine Basic Shop Visit or a Performance Restoration Shop Visit by reference to the OEM Workscope Planning Guide, and maintenance reserves or end-of-lease compensation are often released only for that class of visit.

A hospital visit that a lessee calls a restoration, or a restoration that falls short of the lease definition, is a common source of dispute. Maintenance-reserve clauses and redelivery conditions are the two lease provisions most likely to end in multi-million-dollar arguments. The visit type should be agreed with the lessor before induction, in writing.

sections.heading: Who decides, and when
paragraphs: The decision is made twice. A provisional workscope is drafted from ECM data, borescope findings and LLP status before removal. It is confirmed or changed at table inspection, when the modules are open and the real condition is visible. That second decision is where an independent representative earns their day rate.

Flight Hour Solution compiles and reviews workscopes for CFM56, LEAP, V2500 and PW4000 engines, attends table inspections and reconciles the final invoice against the workscope that was approved. The visit type is the first line of that workscope.

articles.title: LEAP durability kits: when embodiment pays back
articles.excerpt: The LEAP-1A and LEAP-1B now have certified hot-section durability upgrades. Whether to embody them at the next visit is a workscope decision, not a policy.

sections.heading: What has been certified
paragraphs: The LEAP has two separate durability stories. On the LEAP-1A, fuel-nozzle coking is addressed by a reverse-bleed system, and a high-pressure turbine durability kit was certified in December 2024. On the LEAP-1B, a high-pressure turbine and fuel-nozzle durability package was certified in 2026, with full production cut-over expected in early 2027.

Uptake on the 1A has been fast. CFM reported more than 1,200 HPT kits produced in under a year, with about 70 per cent of the LEAP-1A fleet on the reverse-bleed system and 40 per cent on the HPT kit. IBA's H2 2026 update notes LEAP values benefiting from these product improvements.

The claimed effect is large where it matters. GE Aerospace has said that in harsh environments a LEAP-1A stayed on wing about 1.5 years before the update and about four years with it, and that the kit more than doubles time on wing in severe conditions.
Those figures describe severe environments. The gain in benign operations has to be estimated from an operator's own removal history, not read across from the worst case.

sections.heading: Why it is a workscope decision
paragraphs: Embodiment is not free and not instant. It adds parts, labour and test time to a visit that, for a new-generation engine, already runs 150 per cent or more longer than pre-pandemic norms. In the first half of 2026 LEAP-1A project durations fell 8 per cent while LEAP-1B durations rose 5 per cent, so the shop's turnaround differs by variant.

The payback question therefore has four terms: the extra cost and downtime of embodiment now; the avoided cost of an earlier removal later; the value of the extra time on wing in a market where slots wait two to six months; and the residual-value effect on a leased or financed engine.

Each term is engine-specific. An engine due for a full performance restoration anyway, with the core open and the HPT hardware already being replaced, carries a small incremental cost. An engine in for a quick-turn with healthy margins carries the full cost and gains little until its next planned removal.

sections.heading: When embodiment usually pays back
paragraphs: Embodiment tends to pay back when the engine operates in hot or sandy conditions, when the HPT hardware is being replaced in any case, when the lease or financing rewards the upgraded configuration, and when the operator's own removal history shows durability-driven early removals.

It tends not to pay back, or not yet, when the engine is close to a planned lease return where the lessor has not asked for the upgrade, when the shop cannot supply the kit inside the planned turnaround, or when the environment is benign and the next removal is set by LLP limits rather than by hot-section distress.

For lessors the question is symmetrical. An upgraded engine coming back at redelivery may hold its value better; a lessee asked to fund a configuration change the lease did not foresee will push back. Early shop visits and unexpected module swaps are already complicating redelivery conditions that were drafted before these issues appeared.

sections.heading: What to fix before the visit
paragraphs: Three things should be settled before induction. First, the configuration the lessor expects at redelivery, in writing. Second, kit availability and its effect on the quoted turnaround, confirmed by the shop. Third, the model that compares embodiment now with embodiment at the following visit, using the operator's own data rather than fleet averages.

Flight Hour Solution reviews LEAP-1A and LEAP-1B workscopes as an independent party, with no interest in the parts sold or the slot used. The durability decision is written into the workscope with its assumptions, so the invoice can later be reconciled against it.

articles.title: Maintenance reserves versus actual shop visit cost
articles.excerpt: Reserve rates set years ago meet 2026 invoices. Why the gap ends in dispute, and what to do before the redelivery clock starts.

sections.heading: How the gap opens
paragraphs: A maintenance reserve is a payment, per flight hour or cycle, that the lessee makes against the cost of the next major event. The rate is fixed when the lease is signed, usually with an escalation clause. The invoice arrives years later, at the price of that year.

Since 2019 that later price has moved a long way. CFM56 repair costs are up 50 to 75 per cent, hot-section blade prices about 30 per cent, and fan blade prices have doubled since 2020. Whether a reserve rate set before that inflation still covers the event depends on its escalation clause. That is the first number to check.

The gap is not only about price. Early shop visits, unexpected module swaps and reliability issues are complicating redelivery conditions that were not drafted to anticipate them. In 2025 transitions, MRO slots and correct documentation remained the major problems, and airline records standards often differed from lessor expectations.

sections.heading: Why it ends in dispute
paragraphs: Maintenance-reserve clauses and redelivery conditions are the two lease provisions most likely to trigger multi-million-dollar end-of-lease disputes. The arguments concentrate on four points: life-limited-part valuations, deferred defects, incomplete back-to-birth records and where fair wear and tear ends.

Each point has a reserve dimension. LLP valuation decides how much reserve is released for parts replaced. Deferred defects decide whether a visit qualifies as the event the reserve was collected for. Records decide whether the claim can be proven at all. The boundary of wear and tear decides who pays for the rest.

Lenders have joined the conversation. Engine status is now scrutinised more closely, and engine records, LLP status and maintenance forecasts are expected to stay transparent through the lease. An aircraft with serviceable engines, strong records and manageable maintenance exposure may be worth more than a similar aircraft facing engine uncertainty.

sections.heading: Closing the gap before redelivery
paragraphs: The first step is a reserve adequacy check, engine by engine: the reserve balance against a forecast of the next restoration at current prices, with the LLP stack costed cycle by cycle. The check should run at least a year before redelivery, because slot waits alone can run two to six months.

The second step is a records audit. LLP back-to-birth traceability, shop visit reports and release certificates are gathered and gaps are chased while the operator, the shop and the paperwork still exist. A missing document found at redelivery costs far more than one found twelve months earlier.

The third step is to agree the classification of any shop visit inside the redelivery window before induction: whether it is a performance restoration under the lease definition, which modules are included, and how a module swap will be treated. Silence here is where most claims are born.

The fourth step is a claim file built as the visit runs, not afterwards: the approved workscope, table-inspection findings, scrap tags, the invoice reconciled line by line and the test-cell result. A reserve claim presented with that file is settled; one presented without it is negotiated.

sections.heading: Both sides of the lease
paragraphs: The same discipline serves the lessor. Workscope oversight during the lessee's visit protects the residual value the lessor will inherit, and a joint agreement on the event's classification removes the largest single source of end-of-lease argument.

Flight Hour Solution runs maintenance-reserve calculations and claim analysis, LLP back-to-birth audits and redelivery support for airlines and lessors, and is owned by neither an MRO nor a lessor. The work starts with the reserve adequacy check.

articles.title: Used serviceable material: a strategy for 2026
articles.excerpt: USM meets up to 30 per cent of part demand at some shops, while teardown supply has shrunk. What a material policy needs in 2026.

sections.heading: Two numbers that do not agree
paragraphs: Two facts define engine material in 2026. Bain finds that used serviceable material covers up to 30 per cent of part demand at some shops, while OEM parts demand outpaces supply by 10 to 20 per cent. Magnetic Group finds that teardown part harvesting runs about five times below its pre-2020 level.

Demand for USM is therefore high at the moment supply is thin. Delivery delays keep older aircraft flying instead of feeding teardowns: 17,000 orders were unfilled at the start of 2026 and production ended 2025 at 24 per cent below 2019.

Value works the same way. Aircraft with serviceable engines, strong records and manageable maintenance exposure may now be worth more than similar aircraft facing engine uncertainty, which keeps candidate teardown aircraft in service rather than in the parts market.

The price effect is visible in new parts too. CFM56 hot-section blade prices have risen about 30 per cent since 2019 and fan blade prices have doubled since 2020; repair costs on the family are up 50 to 75 per cent. Every workscope now contains a material decision worth a large share of the invoice.

sections.heading: What a material policy has to decide
paragraphs: A material policy answers four questions before the engine is inducted. Which parts may be sourced as USM, and with what documentation. Where PMA parts and DER repairs are acceptable, and where the lease or the lessor forbids them. Who owns the removed material. And who checks the price of each route against the others.

Lease terms often govern the second question: whether PMA parts and DER repairs are permitted on the engine, and on what conditions. A lessee that fits them against the lease creates a redelivery problem larger than the saving. The policy has to be read against every lease in the fleet, not written once for the airline.

Documentation decides whether USM is an asset or a liability. Since the 2023 AOG Technics case of falsified part paperwork, traceability has become the first question buyers and lessors ask. A USM part without a clean release certificate and back-to-birth trace is not a cheaper part; it is a future finding.

sections.heading: Where the saving actually is
paragraphs: The saving is rarely in the headline part price. It sits in the scrap review, where parts condemned by the shop are checked against manual limits and repair options; in material value extraction, where serviceable removed parts are recovered for the owner rather than left with the shop; and in avoiding long-lead new parts that stretch the turnaround.

The decision point is table inspection. That is when the shop's findings, the repair routes, the USM offers and the lead times can be put on one sheet, and when a representative in the room can still change the outcome. After kitting, the material decision has been made by default.

In a market where slot waits run two to six months and OEM parts demand outpaces supply, the schedule value of a USM route can exceed its price value. A part available now, with paperwork, can be worth more than a cheaper part that arrives after the test-cell date.

sections.heading: Who should hold the policy
paragraphs: The shop has an interest in the material it sells and the repairs it performs. The parts broker has an interest in the parts it holds. The policy should therefore sit with the owner or operator, and the check on each route should be done by someone with no stake in which route is chosen.

Flight Hour Solution supports material sourcing and documentation audits, scrap review and material value extraction during shop visits. Where we broker material or an engine ourselves we say so, in line with our conflicts policy, so that the advisory check and the sale are never confused.

articles.title: Engine condition monitoring alerts: pull or watch?
articles.excerpt: An EGT margin alert is a question, not an instruction. How an independent read of ECM and EHM data turns it into a removal decision.

sections.heading: What an alert actually says
paragraphs: Engine condition monitoring watches a small set of cruise parameters over time: exhaust gas temperature margin, fuel flow, core speed, vibration and oil data. An alert means a parameter has shifted against its own trend or a fleet baseline. It does not say why, and it does not say when the engine must come off.

The OEM or the monitoring platform issues the alert and often a recommendation. That recommendation is written for a fleet, from the OEM's view of risk. The operator's question is narrower: this engine, this route network, this LLP position, this slot market.

The distinction matters more in 2026 than it did. Slot waits have lengthened by two to three months, and by up to six, and turnaround times are up 35 per cent or more on legacy engines. An early removal without a slot is an engine on a stand; a late one is an unplanned removal at the worst moment.

sections.heading: Four readings before a decision
paragraphs: First, the rate of change. A step change in EGT margin after a known event, such as a bird strike or a water wash, reads differently from a steady decline over hundreds of cycles. The shape of the trend usually points to the module before a borescope confirms it.

Second, the corroboration. A margin shift with a matching change in fuel flow and core speed is a different case from a lone parameter. Vibration and oil data either support the hot-section story or point elsewhere. One line on a chart is rarely enough to schedule a shop visit.

Third, the borescope. A targeted inspection of the stage the trend implicates turns a statistical signal into a physical finding: distress, coating loss, a crack within or outside limits. The borescope report, not the alert, is what a shop will quote against.

Fourth, the calendar. The remaining margin at the current rate of loss is set against the LLP limits, the next planned removal, spare-engine cover and the slot lead time. If the engine can reach a planned window with margin to spare, watching is a decision, not a delay.

sections.heading: When to pull, when to watch
paragraphs: Pull early when the trend is accelerating, when the borescope finding is close to a limit that would force an unplanned removal, when a slot is available inside the window and a later one is not, or when the LLP position means the visit is coming soon in any case and the workscope can absorb the finding.

Watch when the trend is flat after a known cause, when the finding is well inside limits and repeat inspections are practical, when spare-engine cover is thin and a slot is months away, or when the next planned removal already falls inside the projected margin life.

sections.heading: Why the independent read is worth paying for
paragraphs: Lessors are starting to evaluate how well an aircraft is operated, not only its hours and cycles. A documented history of trend review, timely inspection and reasoned removal decisions reads as a lower-risk asset, and digital maintenance records improve liquidity, financeability and residual values.

That history is easier to produce when each alert is answered with a written read: what the data shows, what was inspected, what was decided and why. The same file supports the workscope at the next visit and the reserve claim after it.

Flight Hour Solution runs ECM and EHM monitoring programmes and on-wing performance reviews for CFM56, LEAP, V2500 and PW4000 fleets, and gives a second opinion on trend alerts and removal timing. The read is independent of the platform vendor, the shop and the OEM.
